doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

title: New Orleans music welcomes every audience: gigs from the Natchez to Bourbon Street
summary: New Orleans music does not apologize for being entertaining. He describes recent jobs on the steamboat Natchez, at Antoine's bar, at a new Bourbon Street club and with his Monday quartet.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: I guess what I started to say is even though we’re not apologizers for the potential for the music to be artistic, we’re also definitely not apologizing for the music to be enjoyed and

the experience. People can enter the experience of New Orleans music on as many levels as they want. I mean I had, before I came up here I worked — when I came up to New York on a Tuesday, I came here to do some of the outreach on Wednesday, which I’m very grateful for, I’m really starting to get where I don’t want to ever just go up and do a concert anymore, I just don’t want to do that, I really think it’s important, especially if there are students that are coming, I really feel like I have a responsibility to let them know something about what they’re going to hear. So I’m really grateful to have that opportunity. But New Orleans music just doesn’t apologize for being entertaining. There’s something about the modern jazz aesthetic to me that seems like there’s either two ways, it’s the, “I’m going to dare you try to enjoy this” or it’s going to be — so there’s that aspect of it, and you sure the hell ain’t going to dance to it, oh no, ut uh. There’s that, and then there’s almost a, “Well what I’m doing is really intellectual but you can enjoy it too.” So there’s two sides of it, where there’s like an apology involved and New Orleans music just doesn’t work on that level. So the three jobs I did before I came up this weekend were: one of them was on the steamboat Natchez playing the dinner cruise, which was beautiful, the river is beautiful at 6:00, the sun is just setting and you’re playing and you go down river and you play a couple of sets of music and people dance or have a beer on the deck of the boat or whatever they want to do. So that was something that has its own forum. I played another club the next night which was just a bar at one of the famous restaurants, Antoine’s, they opened up a new bar facing the street. It’s a terrible room for music. It’s one of those rooms that’s so bad for music that the only time that the music has the chance of becoming good is when there’s nobody there. But of course from a business standpoint that doesn’t work very well. But people can sit a little closer and listen if they want or they can sit a little farther away and talk and have a good time. You don’t have an expectations of what the audience is supposed to be. And then I had another job in one of the new jazz clubs that’s reopened. There’s finally a jazz club on Bourbon Street again. And this club is the same way. It’s big enough that if people want to talk they actually don’t bother you that much. But it’s also big enough that when they talk, depending on where they’re sitting, you can’t really hear what’s happening. And in all those situations, like that last one — and then I had my regular band on Monday, which is a quartet and we turn this bar and it’s like a jazz club the way you think of it. I mean all of a sudden I’ve got 40 people up in there on a Monday night just listening to the music and drinking nice cocktails. Everything is different. And if in any of those situations people wanted to talk or people wanted to dance there is always a place for them to do that. There’s always a place, there’s always an acceptance of them to enter the experience on whatever level they want and to provide a listening experience that can appeal to all those points of entry. If you can appeal to an

aficionado and a tourist that wants to hear “The Saints Go Marching In” — if you can appeal to both those people at the same time because of the level of musicianship, I mean I think that’s when you’ve got success, that’s the best example of when New Orleans music works.
